title: Evaluate a Nested Logic Formula
statement:
A logic formula is written as a string using these forms:

  • t is true and f is false.
  • !(x) is the negation of the formula x.
  • &(x1,x2,...,xk) is true when all of its k ≥ 1 parts are true.
  • |(x1,x2,...,xk) is true when at least one of its k ≥ 1 parts is true.

Parts are separated by commas with no spaces, and parts can themselves be any formula. The input is always well formed. Return the value of the whole formula.

examples.why: !(f) is true and |(f,f,t) is true, so all three parts of the & are true.
&(t,f) is false, so the | has no true part.
One false part makes the & false, and ! flips it.

constraints: formula is well formed and uses only the characters t f ! & | ( ) ,
Brackets nest at most 200 levels deep
hints: The innermost brackets can be evaluated first, without knowing anything about the outside. Which data structure lets you finish the inside and come back to the outside?
Scan left to right and push every character except commas onto a stack. When you see ), everything on top down to the matching ( is a list of already evaluated parts.
Pop those parts, pop the ( and the operator below it, apply the operator, and push the single result back as t or f.

explain.intuition:
A closing bracket is the moment a group becomes complete. At that point every part inside it has already been reduced to a single t or f, so the group can be evaluated and replaced by one value. A stack keeps exactly the unfinished outer groups waiting underneath, the same way a JSON or HTML parser keeps a stack of open tags.

A recursive parser does the same thing with the call stack: parse() reads one formula, and when it sees an operator it calls itself once per part. Both read each character once.
steps: Create an empty stack and scan the formula character by character.
Skip commas. Push any other character except ).
On ): pop values until you reach (, noting whether you saw any t and any f. Pop the (, then pop the operator.
Push the result: for ! the opposite of the single value, for & "no f seen", for | "some t seen".
At the end the stack holds one value; return whether it is t.
pitfalls: Treating ! as taking several parts. It always has exactly one.
Evaluating left to right without respecting the brackets, for example short-circuiting an & and then losing track of where its bracket ends.
Rescanning the whole string for the innermost group after every reduction, which is O(n²) on long inputs.

solutions.title: Reduce innermost groups repeatedly
solutions.idea: Every group with no brackets inside can be evaluated directly. Replace them all with t or f and repeat until one letter is left.

solutions.title: Explicit stack
solutions.idea: Push characters; on a closing bracket, pop the finished parts, apply the operator under them and push the result.

solutions.title: Recursive descent
solutions.idea: parse() reads one formula starting at a shared index; an operator reads its parts by calling parse() again.

followups: Add an operator ^(x1,...,xk) that is true when an odd number of parts are true. What changes in each solution?
Short-circuit: stop evaluating an & at its first false part. How do you skip the rest of its text quickly?
